title: 5 Qube Money Alternatives That Actually Control Your Spending in 2026
summary: Find the best Qube Money alternatives that actually control spending with envelope budgeting. Compare top apps after Qube's transition.
body_text: If you relied on Qube Money to add real structure to your spending, you already know that tracking is not the same as control. Qube Money built a loyal following by making envelope budgeting feel real, helping users choose where money belonged before spending it instead of simply tracking categories after the fact. But as Qube transitions toward Qube+, a budgeting system that connects to an outside checking account rather than holding customer funds, many users are looking for a more stable replacement. The category lost its most recognizable brand when Intuit shut down Mint at the start of 2024, yet the population using personal finance apps weekly has grown to roughly 38% of U.S. adults, the highest share ever recorded by Federal Reserve consumer surveys. That means more people are searching for better options than ever. According to Research and Markets' 2026 Personal Finance Apps Report, the global personal finance app market is valued at $207.69 billion in 2026, so the right tool is absolutely out there. The challenge is finding the one that matches how you actually want to manage money. This guide covers five of the strongest Qube Money alternatives available in 2026, ranked for a general audience that wants spending discipline, not just spending awareness. Key Takeaways Envelope is the closest like-for-like replacement: Envelope is the closest Qube Money alternative because it combines envelope budgeting, card controls, and banking in one app. If intentional spending at the point of sale was the feature you valued most, Envelope replicates it most directly. YNAB delivers the strongest budgeting philosophy, without a debit card: Users who engage consistently with YNAB report saving an average of $6,000 in their first year. At $180/year, that is a 33x return on the subscription cost. If those numbers appeal and you do not need a built-in card, YNAB is worth serious consideration. Goodbudget offers a genuinely free starting point: Goodbudget offers a free tier with up to 10 envelopes and 1 account, enough for basic budgeting. The Plus plan at $10/month or $80/year unlocks unlimited envelopes, accounts, debt tracking, and 7 years of history. Start here before committing to a paid app. Monarch Money suits big-picture trackers, not strict spenders: Spending, savings, investments and net worth all live in one clean app, with the best couples experience of any budgeting tool. It is not built for strict spending discipline, but for financial visibility and awareness it is outstanding. EveryDollar fits Ramsey followers best: EveryDollar is a solid choice if you are a fan of Dave Ramsey's system and want a budgeting app built specifically around zero-based budgeting. For anyone else, the options below will serve you better. Quick-Start Prioritization Framework Use this table to identify your best fit before reading each full entry below. App Best For Effort Level Monthly Cost Time to Results Envelope Intentional spending with a debit card Low Free, $40/year Days YNAB Zero-based budgeting, debt payoff High ~$9.08/mo (annual) Weeks Goodbudget Manual envelope budgeting, beginners Medium Free / $10/mo Days Monarch Money Full financial dashboard, couples Low ~$8.33/mo (annual) Days EveryDollar Ramsey Baby Steps followers Medium Free / $6.67/mo Weeks Start here based on your situation: You want spending control at the register: Envelope, closest to how Qube actually worked. You are paying off debt and want a proven method: YNAB, highest documented savings results. You have never budgeted before and want free: Goodbudget, legitimately usable free tier. You have investments, a mortgage, and multiple accounts: Monarch Money, built for financial visibility. You are following Dave Ramsey's Baby Steps: EveryDollar, purpose-built for that plan. 1. Envelope, Best Overall and Best for Intentional Spending with a Debit Card If you have tried budgeting apps before and given up because the plan never matched your spending, Envelope solves that problem structurally by making your bank account and your budget the same product. That single sentence captures why former Qube users find it the most natural landing spot. How It Works Envelope is the stronger choice for anyone who uses a debit card as their primary payment method and has experienced the frustrating gap between a well-made plan and a bank account that does not know the plan exists. If your core problem is overspending despite making a budget, Envelope solves it structurally by making your budget and your bank account the same thing. You create named envelopes for each spending category, allocate your paycheck before you spend, and the card enforces those limits in real time. What It Costs Envelope's full feature set and pricing details are listed on the Envelope website. The app is designed to be accessible for users moving away from Qube, with a model that does not require juggling a separate bank and a separate tracker. Pros and Cons Pros: Combines banking and budgeting in a single product, eliminating the gap between plan and action Envelope-level card controls work at the point of sale, the same way Qube did Built-in banking rails including check deposits, wires, and cash, features Qube always lacked Purpose-built for displaced Qube users, with a direct migration path Cons: Requires switching your primary checking account, which takes a few days to set up Fewer investment tracking features than Monarch Money Fintech banking requires an adjustment period for users accustomed to traditional banks Pro Tip: If you are migrating from Qube, keep your old account open for two to three weeks while your direct deposit transfers. This prevents any gap in bill payments during the switch. 2. YNAB (You Need A Budget), Best for Zero-Based Budgeting Without a Card YNAB has one of the most devoted user bases in personal finance software. YNAB users are famously loyal, and the 75% twelve-month retention rate is the highest in the budgeting app category. The reason comes down to methodology: YNAB is a personal finance app built around a specific structure called zero-based budgeting. Instead of tracking what you have already spent, YNAB asks you to assign every dollar a job before it leaves your account. What You Get YNAB syncs with more than 12,000 banks, giving users a deeper understanding of their financial situation at any given time. Beyond syncing, the app's educational layer is substantial: the r/ynab subreddit has over 250,000 members in 2026, an active peer community that is surprisingly useful when you hit a methodology question or overspending problem. What It Costs According to The Penny Hoarder's 2026 YNAB review, YNAB costs $14.99/month or $109/year, with a 34-day free trial. That price comes with a meaningful payoff: users who engage consistently report saving an average of $6,000 in their first year, which translates to a 33x return on the subscription cost. If you are not seeing meaningful savings within three months of daily use, revisit your category structure. Pros and Cons Pros: Zero-based framework is genuinely behavior-changing when applied consistently Syncs with over 12,000 financial institutions Up to six people on a single subscription with no extra charge 34-day free trial is one of the longest in the category Cons: The Penny Hoarder's 2026 YNAB review it is one of the more expensive budgeting apps on the market in 2026 No built-in debit card or banking, so discipline relies entirely on the user Learning curve is real, plan for two to four weeks to become comfortable No free tier after the trial period ends Pro Tip: YNAB's annual billing at $109/year saves roughly 39% over monthly billing. Commit to the annual plan only after completing the free trial and verifying the methodology works for your habits. 3. Goodbudget, Best Free Option for Envelope Budgeting Beginners Goodbudget is an app that digitizes the envelope budgeting method, where you allocate money to specific spending categories rather than letting it sit in one general account. The app brings this budgeting system to your phone, eliminating the need for physical envelopes and the risks that go along with them. How It Works Crucially, Goodbudget does not automatically connect to your bank. It is a manual-entry app. You record transactions yourself, by hand, every time you spend. For some users that friction is the whole point, the virtual envelope system is intuitive and psychologically effective: once your "dining" envelope is empty, you stop dining out. What It Costs Goodbudget offers a free tier with up to 10 envelopes and one account. The Plus plan at $10/month or $80/year unlocks unlimited envelopes, accounts, debt tracking, and seven years of history. According to FinanceApps.guide's Goodbudget review, the app holds a 4.5/5 rating from 22,000 users, a strong signal for an app in this category. Pros and Cons Pros: Free tier is genuinely functional, not just a demo Manual entry builds real spending awareness with every transaction Syncs across up to five devices for couples budgeting together Available on iOS, Android, and web Cons: The interface feels dated compared to newer apps. Reporting is basic, there is no bank sync even on the paid plan, and the free tier's 10-envelope limit can feel restrictive. No debit card integration, so the plan and your spending are always separate You have to enter every transaction yourself, a deal-breaker for some and a deliberate choice for others, according to FinCompareLab's 2026 Goodbudget review 4. Monarch Money, Best for Full Financial Visibility Monarch Money sits near the top of every "best budgeting app" list right now. When Mint shut down in March 2024, millions of budgeters were left scrambling for a new home for their money, and Monarch Money quickly emerged as one of the most popular replacements. How It Works The app combines flexible budgeting (both zero-based and traditional tracking), comprehensive account aggregation, investment tracking, and collaborative features for households. Where Qube was tightly focused on spending control, Monarch takes the opposite approach: it gives you a panoramic view of your entire financial life in one place. What It Costs At $14.99 per month or $99.99 per year for its Core plan or $199 per year for Plus, Monarch remains one of the pricier personal finance apps on the market. The Core plan is sufficient for most users. As noted in At $14.99 per month or $99.99 per, the Core plan at $99.99/year includes unlimited account syncing, the AI Assistant, and shared household access for couples, everything most users will actually need. Pros and Cons Pros: The app syncs with 15,000+ institutions and provides detailed net worth tracking, spending analytics, and savings goal management Best couples and household experience of any app in this category AI assistant lets you ask plain-English questions about your spending Investment and net worth tracking closes a gap that YNAB does not fill Cons: No free tier, only a 7-day trial before payment is required It is not built for strict spending discipline, users who want hard spending limits at the register will find it too passive $99 per year for a single-person household is steep next to cheaper alternatives No built-in debit card or direct spending controls 5. EveryDollar, Best for Dave Ramsey Followers EveryDollar combines budget creation, expense tracking, and integration with Ramsey's debt payoff methodologies (Baby Steps), making it ideal for those following the Ramsey financial plan or seeking aggressive debt elimination. If that describes you, it is one of the most purpose-built tools available. How It Works The core method is simple: give every dollar a job before the month starts. Income minus all assigned expenses and savings equals zero. The 2026 relaunch added meaningful new features for premium subscribers, including the Margin Finder tool. According to FinCompareLab's EveryDollar review, EveryDollar relaunched in January 2026 with four meaningful new Premium features, the most notable being Margin Finder, a guided 15-minute questionnaire that surfaces budget leaks. What It Costs EveryDollar is free to download with basic features. Premium costs $79.99 per year or $17.99 per month, with a 14-day free trial. The free tier is enough to test the zero-based method manually. However, the feature most people actually want, automatic bank syncing, sits behind the paywall. If you plan to use the app long-term, budget for the annual plan. Pros and Cons Pros: Free tier is functional for manual zero-based budgeting Guided integration with Ramsey's Baby Steps framework for debt payoff Debt-free date calculator updates in real time as you make payments Straightforward interface, easy to set up in under 30 minutes Cons: EveryDollar is basic. You cannot use it for investment monitoring, retirement planning, bill payments, or credit score monitoring. Unlike YNAB's broader applicability, EveryDollar assumes a specific financial philosophy; it works poorly if you do not follow the Ramsey approach Premium plan is not available outside the United States No debit card or banking integration of any kind Pro Tip: Use EveryDollar's free tier for a full month before paying for Premium. If you find yourself manually entering every transaction and not skipping any, that is a strong signal you will actually use the bank sync feature enough to justify the upgrade. How to Choose: Common Situations Mapped to the Right App You used Qube because it made you pause before spending Envelope is your app. If you used Qube because it helped you pause, choose a category, and spend with purpose, Envelope is the most natural replacement. The debit card enforcement is the key feature, none of the other apps on this list replicate it. You want the most proven savings results Go with YNAB. If you are motivated to change your financial behavior fundamentally and willing to invest time in a methodology, YNAB offers the highest documented return. Plan two to four weeks for the learning curve before you judge the results. You want to see your full financial picture in one place Monarch Money is built for this. After a 30-day hands-on test with real bank accounts, credit cards, investments, and a mortgage, Monarch Money is one of the best all-in-one personal finance apps available in 2026, especially for users who want a comprehensive financial picture in one place. Frequently Asked Questions Why are people looking for Qube Money alternatives in 2026? Qube has transitioned away from its original banking model. Qube's own FAQ stated that scheduled payments and transfers would stop after September 30, 2025, and Qube+ is described as a system that connects to an outside checking account rather than holding customer funds itself. This shift has left many users searching for a replacement that maintains the same level of spending control. Which Qube alternative is closest to how Qube actually worked? Envelope is the closest match. Many Qube users tried some of the more common alternatives, but found themselves still juggling multiple apps or giving up on discipline. Envelope is built differently. It combines budgeting, card controls, and banking in a single product rather than layering a tracker on top of a separate bank account. Is there a free Qube Money alternative? Yes. Goodbudget is the strongest free option for envelope-style budgeting without a bank connection. Its free tier gives you 10 envelopes and full access to the manual entry workflow at no cost. EveryDollar also offers a genuinely functional free tier for zero-based budgeting, though bank sync requires its paid plan. Do any of these alternatives require switching my bank account? Most do not. YNAB, Goodbudget, Monarch Money, and EveryDollar all connect to your existing accounts without requiring you to move your money. Envelope does require using its built-in checking account, but that is precisely what gives it debit card-level spending control, the feature Qube users most want to preserve. How much should I expect to pay for a quality budgeting app in 2026? The range is wide. Goodbudget and EveryDollar offer functional free tiers. Mid-tier options like Monarch Money Core run approximately $8.33/month billed annually. The Penny Hoarder's 2026 YNAB review YNAB is among the more expensive budgeting apps in 2026. As a general rule: if a paid app helps you spend even 1% more intentionally on a $50,000 income, it pays for itself within months. Final Verdict The right Qube alternative depends entirely on what you valued most about Qube. If the answer is "a debit card that enforces my budget categories," choose Envelope. If the answer is "a structured method for assigning every dollar a job," YNAB is the most proven option. If you are starting fresh and want to try envelope budgeting for free before committing, Goodbudget is your on-ramp. The average personal savings rate sits at just 2.6% in 2026, and 49% of Americans would struggle to cover a $400 emergency expense today. A budgeting system that actually holds at the register, not just on a spreadsheet, is one of the most effective tools available for closing that gap. title: The History of AI Benchmarks: Why Every Model Claims to Be the Best (2026)
summary: The complete history of AI benchmarks, from the Turing test to ARC-AGI-2. Why benchmarks saturate, how contamination inflates scores, and what to trust.
body_text: A BENCHMARK CLAIM WHAT IT LEAVES OUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── "72% on SWE-bench Verified" → Which harness? Tools? Retries? Same scaffold as the comparison? "Beats the leading model on MMLU" → By how much? Inside noise? Which of the 57 subjects moved? "State of the art on ARC-AGI" → At what cost per task? $2 or $4,000 is the whole story. "Human-level performance" → Which humans? Experts or crowd? Measured how, on which subset? "#1 on the leaderboard" → Self-reported or reproduced? How many private attempts first? ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── RULE OF THUMB: a score without a harness, a cost, and a date is a press release, not a measurement.

title: Postpartum Health Problems: A Complete Guide from an Internal Medicine Doctor
summary: Fatigue, mood changes, and hair loss after birth can be normal recovery or a sign of thyroiditis, anemia, or PPD. An internal medicine doctor explains how to tell the difference.
body_text: The postpartum period is one of the most medically volatile windows in a woman's life, and it's treated like a footnote. Estrogen and progesterone crash. Thyroid function destabilizes. Iron stores may be depleted. The immune system recalibrates. And all of that is happening while she's sleep-deprived, physically recovering, and being told by everyone around her that what she's feeling is just part of being a new mom. The problem is that the symptoms of normal postpartum recovery overlap almost perfectly with the symptoms of conditions that need treatment. You can't tell them apart by how they feel. You can only tell them apart by checking. Start a chat with Dr Shirin Syed Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. The short version After delivery, the body goes through a dramatic hormonal shift that can cause fatigue, mood changes, hair loss, and heart palpitations as part of normal recovery. But those same symptoms are also how postpartum thyroiditis, iron-deficiency anemia, postpartum depression and anxiety, and postpartum cardiomyopathy present. The overlap is nearly complete, which is why these conditions get missed constantly. The standard postpartum visit happens at six weeks, which is too early to catch conditions that present at three, six, or even nine months. Diagnosis starts with basic labs (a complete blood count for iron status, a thyroid panel with TSH and free T4) and validated screening for postpartum mood disorders. Most of this is orderable and interpretable through a chat consultation. Treatment depends on the condition: iron repletion for anemia (noticeable improvement in 2 to 4 weeks), levothyroxine for hypothyroid-phase thyroiditis (4 to 6 weeks to feel a shift), SSRIs for postpartum depression (2 to 4 weeks for initial effect, full response at 6 to 8 weeks). The trajectory matters more than any single symptom. Normal postpartum fatigue gradually improves. If it's getting worse at 8 or 10 weeks, that's a signal to investigate. Table of contents What's actually happening in the postpartum body Who gets missed (and why it keeps happening) The signs and symptoms, and what they're often confused with How these conditions get diagnosed Treatment landscape What treatment actually feels like, week to week Side effects, monitoring, and how the plan adjusts Lifestyle and self-management: what actually moves the needle (and what doesn't) Complications and what to watch for When to seek care vs. wait it out The honest take Frequently asked questions What's actually happening in the postpartum body During pregnancy, estrogen and progesterone climb to levels the body has never seen before. They support the placenta, suppress certain immune pathways, increase blood volume by nearly 50%, and reshape almost every organ system. Then delivery happens, and within 24 to 48 hours, those hormones plummet. It's one of the most abrupt hormonal transitions in human biology. That crash sets off a cascade. The thyroid, which was working overtime during pregnancy, can destabilize. In some women, the immune system mounts an inflammatory response against the thyroid gland itself, a condition called postpartum thyroiditis. Blood volume contracts. If there was significant bleeding during or after delivery, iron stores may already be depleted. The brain, meanwhile, is adjusting to a hormonal environment that looks nothing like what it had for the past nine months, which is the biological setup for postpartum mood disorders. And this is what makes it so tricky: every single one of those processes produces symptoms that look exactly like what you'd expect from sleep deprivation and the stress of caring for a newborn. Fatigue. Brain fog. Mood swings. Hair shedding. Heart racing. The biology that makes postpartum recovery hard is the same biology that creates the window for real pathology. You cannot separate them by how they feel. You separate them by running the right labs and asking the right questions. Who gets missed (and why it keeps happening) Postpartum health problems don't discriminate by age, parity, or delivery method. But certain patterns make some women more likely to be missed. First-time mothers are the most vulnerable to the normalization trap. They have no baseline for comparison. When everyone tells them "this is just what it's like," they have no prior experience to push back with. A second-time mom who felt fine after her first baby and feels terrible after her second is more likely to flag something. A first-time mom assumes terrible is the default. Women with a history of autoimmune conditions (Hashimoto's, type 1 diabetes, lupus) have a significantly higher risk of postpartum thyroiditis, but many aren't screened for it unless they specifically ask. The connection between autoimmune history and postpartum thyroid dysfunction is well established, but it doesn't always make it into the postpartum visit conversation. Women who had significant blood loss during delivery , whether from hemorrhage, C-section, or even a normal vaginal delivery with moderate bleeding, are at risk for iron-deficiency anemia that their prenatal vitamin alone won't fix. The fatigue from anemia is indistinguishable from the fatigue of sleep deprivation unless someone checks a lab. Black women in the US face a compounding problem. They have significantly higher rates of postpartum complications, including maternal mortality, and a documented pattern of having their symptoms dismissed or minimized by the healthcare system [per CDC Maternal Mortality data]. When a Black woman says "something doesn't feel right," she is statistically less likely to be taken seriously. That's a systemic failure, not a medical mystery. The structural reason these conditions get missed is simple: the system gives new moms one postpartum visit at six weeks and acts like that's sufficient. Six weeks. The body is still in upheaval. Postpartum thyroiditis can present at three months. Postpartum depression can present at six months. The system is designed around the baby's pediatric visit schedule, not the mother's health. The baby gets seen at 2 weeks, 1 month, 2 months, 4 months, 6 months. The mom gets one appointment and a "good luck." The signs and symptoms, and what they're often confused with Crushing fatigue that doesn't improve with rest. Every new mom is tired. But the fatigue from iron-deficiency anemia or hypothyroidism has a different quality. It's disproportionate. It's the kind where you sleep for six hours (a luxury) and wake up feeling like you didn't sleep at all. It doesn't gradually lift as the baby starts sleeping longer. It sits on you. When fatigue is getting worse at 8, 10, 12 weeks postpartum instead of slowly improving, that's not normal adjustment. That's a signal. It gets confused with garden-variety sleep deprivation, and the confusion matters because the treatment for anemia (iron repletion) and the treatment for thyroid dysfunction (levothyroxine) are specific and effective, while the treatment for sleep deprivation (more sleep) isn't available to a woman caring for a newborn. Hair loss. Postpartum hair shedding, telogen effluvium, is real. During pregnancy, high estrogen keeps hair in its growth phase. After delivery, the hormonal drop triggers a synchronized shedding phase, usually peaking around 3 to 4 months postpartum. That part is normal and self-limiting. But hair loss that's severe, that starts early, or that doesn't resolve by 6 to 9 months can also be a sign of iron deficiency or thyroid dysfunction. Writing it all off as "hormonal" means you might miss something treatable that's making it worse or making it last longer. Heart palpitations and a racing heart. The postpartum thyroid can swing into a hyperthyroid phase before settling into hypothyroidism. During the hyperthyroid phase, heart palpitations, a tremor, anxiety, and heat intolerance are common. These get attributed to the stress of new motherhood and the caffeine a new mom is relying on to function. The distinction matters because the hyperthyroid phase of postpartum thyroiditis is usually self-limiting and monitored, while a racing heart from postpartum cardiomyopathy is a medical emergency. Mood changes: sadness, numbness, irritability, rage. The "baby blues" are real and affect up to 80% of new mothers in the first two weeks [per ACOG]. They resolve on their own. Postpartum depression is different. It's persistent. It deepens. It can present as sadness, but it can also present as numbness, irritability, or a flat affect that doesn't match what the mom expected to feel. The confusion between baby blues and postpartum depression costs women months of suffering because the assumption is "this will pass" when it won't without treatment. Severe anxiety and intrusive thoughts. Postpartum anxiety disorder is underdiagnosed because some degree of worry about a newborn seems reasonable. But the clinical version is consuming. It's checking the baby's breathing every 10 minutes. It's being unable to let anyone else hold the baby. It's intrusive thoughts about harm coming to the baby that play on a loop. That's not "normal new mom worry." That's a condition, and it responds to treatment. Normalizing it as just part of motherhood keeps women from getting help. Shortness of breath and swelling. Mild swelling can linger postpartum. But progressive shortness of breath with minimal exertion, swelling that's getting worse, and difficulty lying flat are symptoms of postpartum cardiomyopathy, a rare but serious condition where the heart muscle weakens. It gets written off as deconditioning. It shouldn't be. How these conditions get diagnosed The workup for a new mom whose symptoms aren't improving on the expected trajectory starts with two things: the right labs and the right questions. Labs: A complete blood count (CBC) to check hemoglobin and a ferritin level to assess iron stores. Hemoglobin can be "normal" while ferritin is in the single digits, which means the body's iron reserves are depleted even if the blood count hasn't dropped yet. A thyroid panel, TSH and free T4 at minimum. TSH alone can miss the picture if she's in the hyperthyroid phase of postpartum thyroiditis. These are standard outpatient labs, orderable through a chat consultation without needing to step into a clinic. Screening for postpartum mood disorders: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a validated 10-question screening tool that takes a few minutes. It's not a diagnosis, but it's a reliable flag. The questions that don't get asked enough, and should be asked directly because most new moms won't volunteer it: "Are you having thoughts that scare you? Are you feeling like yourself? Is this getting better or worse?" Those questions open the door for a woman who has been white-knuckling it in silence. History and trajectory are the most diagnostic tools here. The pattern matters more than any single symptom. Is the fatigue improving, stable, or worsening? Did symptoms start suddenly or build gradually? Is there a symptom that feels disproportionate to the sleep deprivation? A detailed history, taken over chat where there's no 15-minute clock, often surfaces the pattern that a rushed in-person visit misses. Most of what matters for diagnosing postpartum health problems is doable through chat: the history, the labs, the screening tools, the trajectory tracking. If something in the picture raises concern for postpartum cardiomyopathy (progressive shortness of breath, worsening swelling, inability to lie flat), your FutureClinic doctor can recommend in-person evaluation for cardiac imaging. But that's the escalation path for a specific subset, not the default. In most presentations, the answer starts with labs and a real conversation. Start a chat with Dr Shirin Syed Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. Treatment landscape Iron-deficiency anemia. First-line is oral iron supplementation, typically ferrous sulfate or ferrous bisglycinate (which tends to cause less nausea). The dose matters, the timing matters (take it with vitamin C, not with coffee, tea, or calcium), and the duration matters: full repletion takes a couple of months even after symptoms start improving. For severe depletion or women who can't tolerate oral iron, IV iron infusion is the step up. Postpartum thyroiditis. Treatment depends on the phase. The initial hyperthyroid phase (if it occurs) is usually self-limiting and managed with symptom control, a beta-blocker for palpitations and tremor if needed. If she transitions into the hypothyroid phase, levothyroxine is the standard treatment. Some women's thyroid function normalizes within a year; others develop permanent hypothyroidism and stay on levothyroxine long-term. Monitoring with repeat thyroid panels determines the trajectory. Postpartum depression and anxiety. SSRIs are the first-line pharmacologic treatment. Sertraline is the most commonly prescribed because it has the most safety data in breastfeeding women [per LactMed / NIH]. Therapy, specifically cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), has strong evidence as a standalone or adjunct treatment. For severe cases, particularly with psychotic features or active suicidal ideation, urgent psychiatric evaluation is needed. Postpartum cardiomyopathy. This is managed by cardiology, typically with heart failure medications (beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics). It requires in-person cardiac evaluation and monitoring. This is the condition in this landscape where the chat consultation's role is recognition and triage, not ongoing management. I don't have a financial incentive to push one treatment over another. The consultation is what I charge for, so the recommendation reflects what fits your situation, not a formulary or a product line. That's worth naming because a lot of postpartum health content online is downstream of companies selling a specific supplement or medication. What treatment actually feels like, week to week Iron repletion. The first thing most women notice is that the nausea from the supplement is real, especially with ferrous sulfate on an empty stomach. Taking it with a small amount of food (not dairy) and vitamin C helps. Energy improvement usually becomes noticeable around weeks 2 to 4. It's not dramatic at first. It's more like the heaviness lifts a little. Full repletion, where ferritin is back in a healthy range, takes 2 to 3 months of consistent supplementation. A repeat ferritin at the 2-month mark tells you whether the dose and absorption are working. Levothyroxine for hypothyroid-phase thyroiditis. The medication takes time. Most women notice cognitive symptoms (brain fog, difficulty concentrating) start to lift in the first 2 to 4 weeks. Energy and temperature regulation follow over 6 to 12 weeks. The first dose adjustment usually happens around week 6 to 8, based on a repeat TSH. Some women need one adjustment; some need two or three before the dose is right. You'll have one morning where you wake up and something feels slightly lighter. That's the signal. SSRIs for postpartum depression. The honest timeline: the first 1 to 2 weeks can feel worse before they feel better. Side effects like nausea, headache, or increased anxiety are common in the startup phase and typically settle by week 2 to 3. The therapeutic effect, the actual mood shift, usually begins around weeks 2 to 4, with full effect at 6 to 8 weeks. If there's no meaningful improvement by week 6 to 8 at an adequate dose, that's when the conversation about adjusting the dose or switching medications happens. On FutureClinic, that trajectory isn't a one-shot conversation. Your same doctor is in the chat as you experience it, so the dose adjustment that matters happens when the pattern is visible, not at a follow-up appointment you had to schedule six weeks out and find childcare for. Side effects, monitoring, and how the plan adjusts Oral iron causes constipation and nausea in a meaningful percentage of women. Switching from ferrous sulfate to ferrous bisglycinate often helps with GI tolerance. Taking it every other day instead of daily can improve absorption and reduce side effects without significantly slowing repletion [per Stoffel et al., Lancet Haematology 2017]. Black stools are expected and not a concern. If oral iron isn't tolerated at all, IV iron is the alternative. Levothyroxine is generally well tolerated at the right dose. Symptoms of overreplacement (too high a dose) include palpitations, tremor, insomnia, and anxiety, which can be confusing in a postpartum woman who may already have those symptoms from other causes. Underreplacement means persistent fatigue and brain fog. The monitoring is straightforward: TSH checked 6 to 8 weeks after starting or adjusting, then periodically once stable. The timing of the medication matters: take it on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before food, and separate from iron supplements and calcium by at least 4 hours. SSRIs carry a risk of sexual side effects, weight changes, and emotional blunting in some women. Sertraline specifically can cause GI symptoms (nausea, diarrhea) in the first week or two. The most important monitoring point is the startup phase: if anxiety worsens significantly in the first two weeks, that's worth flagging to your doctor immediately rather than waiting it out. For breastfeeding mothers, sertraline's low transfer into breast milk is well documented, but the conversation about risks and benefits should be individualized. Lifestyle and self-management: what actually moves the needle (and what doesn't) Three things that matter, and one thing that doesn't matter as much as the internet suggests. If you had any significant bleeding during or after delivery, you probably need a dedicated iron supplement. The prenatal vitamin alone isn't enough. Prenatal vitamins typically contain 27 to 30 mg of elemental iron. Therapeutic repletion doses are 60 to 120 mg of elemental iron. That's a meaningful gap. Take the iron with vitamin C (a glass of orange juice works) and away from coffee, tea, and calcium supplements, which block absorption. Track your mood, even if it's just one word a day. Open the notes app on your phone. Write one word for how you felt that day. Do it for two weeks. If you look back and every entry says "terrible" or "numb" or "angry," that's data. That's something you bring to your doctor. It takes the conversation from "I think I might not be doing great" to "here's what the last two weeks looked like." That specificity changes the quality of the clinical response. If something feels wrong in your body, not just tired, but wrong , say it out loud to someone. Your partner, your mom, a friend, your doctor. The act of saying it out loud is the first step to getting it taken seriously. You are not being dramatic. You are not failing at motherhood. You might just need a blood test. What doesn't move the needle as much as social media suggests: "postpartum healing" supplement stacks, placenta encapsulation, and generic "self-care" advice. There's no rigorous evidence that placenta encapsulation improves postpartum mood or energy. Most postpartum supplement stacks are repackaged prenatal vitamins at a higher price point. And telling a sleep-deprived new mom to "prioritize self-care" without addressing the underlying medical question is like telling someone with a broken leg to think positive. The medical question comes first. Start a chat with Dr Shirin Syed Free Describe your symptoms and get real medical guidance, on your schedule. Complications and what to watch for The pattern that concerns me most is the slow burn. It's the mom who comes in at 9 months postpartum, sometimes a year, and she's been white-knuckling it. She's exhausted in a way that goes beyond sleep deprivation. Her hair has thinned significantly. She's been told by everyone, her partner, her mother, her friends, sometimes even her OB, that this is just what it's like now. And when you finally check her labs, her ferritin is in the single digits, or her thyroid is completely off. She's been suffering for months with something that was treatable the whole time. Untreated iron-deficiency anemia doesn't just cause fatigue. Prolonged depletion affects cognitive function, exercise tolerance, immune function, and can worsen postpartum depression. Severe anemia can cause tachycardia and shortness of breath that mimics cardiac disease. Untreated postpartum thyroiditis can progress to permanent hypothyroidism in roughly 20 to 30% of cases [per Stagnaro-Green, JCEM 2012]. Even in cases that eventually resolve, months of untreated hypothyroidism mean months of preventable fatigue, cognitive difficulty, and mood disruption during a period that's already demanding everything she has. Untreated postpartum depression affects the mother and the baby. Maternal depression in the first year is associated with impaired bonding, delayed infant cognitive and emotional development, and increased risk of recurrent depression in the mother [per Slomian et al., J Clin Med 2019]. Early treatment shortens the episode and improves outcomes for both. When to seek care vs. wait it out Three tiers, in this order. This is an emergency. Go to the ER or call 911. If you have any of the following, this is not a chat consultation situation. Go to the nearest emergency room or call 911: Chest pain or severe shortness of breath , especially at rest or with minimal activity. That's postpartum cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise. Severe headache that won't go away, especially with visual changes or elevated blood pressure. Postpartum preeclampsia can happen weeks after delivery, and most people don't realize that. Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. That is an emergency, full stop, and there is no shame in it. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to the nearest ER. Heavy bleeding that soaks through a pad in an hour or less. High fever with chills , possible postpartum infection (endometritis, mastitis with sepsis). Sudden severe leg swelling or pain on one side. Postpartum blood clot risk is real and peaks in the first 6 weeks. None of these are "just adjusting." Do not start a chat for these. This is worth a doctor, and this is what the chat consultation is for Fatigue that's getting worse, not better, at 6 to 8 weeks postpartum. Hair loss that seems excessive or isn't slowing down by 6 months. Heart palpitations or a racing heart at rest. Persistent sadness, numbness, irritability, or anxiety that isn't lifting. Intrusive thoughts that feel consuming or scary. Difficulty bonding with your baby. Any symptom that feels disproportionate to the sleep deprivation. This is the tier that most often gets ignored, and it's worth being honest about why. Most new moms skip care here because of the logistics. Taking time off from caring for a newborn. Finding childcare for an appointment. Scheduling weeks out. Sitting in a waiting room. Those are the real barriers, and women end up telling themselves "it's probably fine" instead of checking. The result, often, is months of frustration, because what looked like normal exhaustion was actually iron deficiency, or what felt like adjustment anxiety was actually postpartum thyroiditis, and both have specific, effective treatments. A chat consultation is real healthcare: real diagnoses, prescriptions, labs, between you and a real doctor, just through chat. You start it from your phone whenever you're ready, usually with a response back the same day. You don't need to find a babysitter, take time off, or sit in a waiting room. And if life interrupts (because you have a newborn), you step away and pick the thread back up later. You can keep trying to figure this out yourself with online resources and forum posts, or you can spend the same fifteen minutes in a chat with a real doctor who can order the right labs, interpret them with you, and write the prescription if that's where this leads. I can manage this with information for now Baby blues in the first two weeks. Mood swings, tearfulness, feeling overwhelmed. These are expected and typically self-limiting. If they persist past two weeks or deepen, move to the tier above. Mild hair shedding starting around 3 to 4 months. Likely telogen effluvium. Expected. Monitor for severity and duration. General fatigue that's proportionate to how much sleep you're getting and is gradually improving as the baby's sleep consolidates. The honest take Before I became a mom, I understood postpartum recovery intellectually. I knew the physiology. I knew the conditions. After going through it, the whole framework shifted. What changed wasn't the medical knowledge. What changed was understanding how easy it is for real pathology to hide behind the assumption that everything is "just postpartum." And how much courage it takes for a new mom to say "I think something is wrong" when everyone around her is saying "this is just how it is." We give new moms one postpartum visit at six weeks and act like that's sufficient. The baby gets seen at 2 weeks, 1 month, 2 months, 4 months, 6 months. The mom gets one appointment. The system is designed around the baby's pediatric schedule, not the mother's health. The baby was the patient. The mom was just the delivery system. That's changing, but slowly. What I want every new mom reading this to hear: struggling postpartum is not a character flaw. It's often a medical condition. And naming it, saying out loud, "I don't think this is normal," is the bravest thing you can do. Just because something is common doesn't mean it's something you should push through. It might just mean nobody checked. Frequently asked questions Is it normal to feel this exhausted as a new mom? Some degree of fatigue is expected when you're sleeping in fragmented stretches. But fatigue that's getting worse instead of gradually improving, that feels disproportionate to the sleep you're losing, or that doesn't lift even on days when you get more rest is worth investigating. A CBC and ferritin level can rule out anemia, and a thyroid panel can rule out postpartum thyroiditis. Both are simple labs. It's better to check and have them come back normal than to assume everything is fine and miss something treatable. Can postpartum depression start months after delivery? Yes. Postpartum depression can present any time in the first year after delivery, and in some cases beyond that [per ACOG Committee Opinion 757]. It doesn't always start in the first few weeks. A woman who felt fine at her six-week visit can develop symptoms at three, six, or nine months. This is one of the reasons a single postpartum visit is insufficient. Is postpartum hair loss always normal? Telogen effluvium, the synchronized shedding triggered by the postpartum hormone drop, is common and self-limiting. It usually peaks around 3 to 4 months and resolves by 9 to 12 months. But hair loss that's severe, that starts unusually early, or that persists beyond a year can also be driven by iron deficiency or thyroid dysfunction. Both are treatable. Checking a ferritin and TSH is a simple way to rule them out. I'm breastfeeding. Can I take an antidepressant? Sertraline (Zoloft) is the most studied SSRI in breastfeeding women and has very low transfer into breast milk [per LactMed database, NIH]. It's generally considered compatible with breastfeeding. The decision should be individualized, but "I'm breastfeeding" is not a reason to suffer through untreated postpartum depression. The risks of untreated depression to both mother and baby are well documented. What's the difference between baby blues and postpartum depression? Baby blues affect up to 80% of new mothers, start within the first few days after delivery, and resolve by about two weeks. They involve mood swings, tearfulness, and feeling overwhelmed. Postpartum depression is persistent, doesn't self-resolve, and often includes symptoms beyond sadness: numbness, irritability, loss of interest, difficulty bonding, changes in sleep or appetite beyond what the baby's schedule explains, and sometimes intrusive thoughts. If mood symptoms persist beyond two weeks or are worsening, that's the line where screening and evaluation should happen. Is it normal that I don't feel bonded to my baby? Bonding isn't always instant. It doesn't always look like the movies. Many women feel a connection that builds gradually over weeks or months, and that's within the range of normal. But if the lack of bonding is accompanied by persistent sadness, numbness, intrusive thoughts, or a feeling of detachment that concerns you, it may be a symptom of postpartum depression. You are not a bad mom for feeling that way. It's a common presentation of a treatable condition. Should I get my thyroid checked postpartum? If you have symptoms like fatigue that isn't improving, hair loss, heart palpitations, mood changes, or unexplained weight changes, a thyroid panel (TSH and free T4) is a reasonable and simple first step. Women with a personal or family history of autoimmune conditions, prior thyroid problems, or type 1 diabetes are at higher risk for postpartum thyroiditis and should have a lower threshold for screening. This is a standard lab that can be ordered through a chat consultation. My iron supplement makes me nauseous. What can I do? Switch from ferrous sulfate to ferrous bisglycinate, which is generally better tolerated. Taking it every other day instead of daily can improve both absorption and side effects [per Stoffel et al., Lancet Haematology 2017]. Take it with vitamin C and away from coffee, tea, and calcium. If oral iron isn't tolerable at all, IV iron is an effective alternative. Don't just stop taking it without telling your doctor. The depletion won't fix itself, and there are workarounds. How do I know if what I'm experiencing is something a doctor should look at? The simplest filter: trajectory. Normal postpartum recovery gradually improves. If your symptoms are stable or worsening at 6 to 8 weeks, if there's a symptom that feels out of proportion to the sleep deprivation, or if you have a persistent feeling that something is off, that's enough to warrant a conversation. You don't need to have a dramatic symptom to deserve a medical opinion. A chat consultation can help sort out whether labs are needed and what the next step looks like for your specific situation. Are postpartum complications more dangerous for Black women? Yes. Black women in the US have maternal mortality rates roughly three times higher than white women, and a significant driver is the documented pattern of their symptoms being dismissed or minimized [per CDC MMWR, 2019]. This isn't a biological inevitability. It's a systemic failure. If you're a Black woman postpartum and something doesn't feel right, your instinct is valid, and you deserve a doctor who takes it seriously. Can postpartum preeclampsia really happen after delivery? Yes. Postpartum preeclampsia can develop up to 6 weeks after delivery, even in women who had normal blood pressure during pregnancy [per ACOG Practice Bulletin 222]. Symptoms include severe headache, visual changes (blurred vision, seeing spots), upper abdominal pain, and significantly elevated blood pressure. This is an emergency. If you have these symptoms, go to the ER. Bottom line The postpartum period is medically complex, and the system currently handles it with one visit and a lot of assumptions. Fatigue, hair loss, mood changes, and a racing heart can all be part of normal recovery. They can also be signs of conditions that have specific, effective treatments. You can't tell the difference by how they feel. You can only tell the difference by checking. If something feels wrong, not just tired, but wrong , say it out loud. Track your symptoms. And if you want a personalized plan for your specific situation, you can start a chat consultation with me through FutureClinic. It's real healthcare, through chat, and I stay with you through the whole process. This article is intended as educational information, not personal medical advice. For one-to-one guidance on your specific situation, talk to your own doctor, or start a chat consultation with a FutureClinic doctor and get a real, personalized answer for your case. title: How Salesforce Eliminated Single-Region Risk and Reduced Downtime Blast Radius at 4B Metrics/Min
summary: Learn how Salesforce re-architected its observability platform to eliminate single-region risk, reduce blast radius, and scale to 4B metrics per minute.
body_text: By Priyanka Singla, Aaron Stockton, and Vincent Poon In our Engineering Energizers Q&A series, we highlight the engineering minds driving innovation across Salesforce. Today, we spotlight Priyanka Singla, Senior Software Engineer on our Argus team, who operates and evolves the internal observability platform ingesting approximately 4 billion metrics per minute for thousands of engineering teams. Explore how the team scaled ingestion, storage, and query performance as telemetry volume grew across Salesforce systems, while also overcoming a single-region AWS dependency, whose blast radius could take down Argus visibility globally. What is your team’s mission in building and operating Argus as Salesforce’s internal observability platform? The team provides Salesforce with an enterprise-grade metrics platform for monitoring, dashboards, and operational visibility. Argus ingests telemetry from services across the company and stores that data at a massive scale. This makes information queryable for teams that depend on fast, reliable insight. That mission extends beyond storage because the platform allows for simple onboarding. Teams adopt Argus without complex integrations or heavy setup. Once they finish onboarding, these teams gain dashboards, alerting, and metrics analysis through a common internal platform. The team also operates Argus as a continuously evolving product. As telemetry patterns shift and new workloads emerge, the architecture expands while maintaining reliability. For thousands of internal users, Argus remains a primary source of metrics visibility across Salesforce services. What scalability pressures emerge when ingesting and storing 4 billion metrics per minute, and how has Argus evolved to keep pace with that growth? The primary scalability demand stems from the fact that observability growth rarely slows. As more services launch and systems become more distributed, telemetry becomes more granular and metric volume rises. Argus now handles roughly 4 billion metrics per minute, which creates significant load across ingestion, storage, and query serving layers. At that throughput, ingestion is only the first constraint. The platform must also store and retrieve data efficiently: Argus retains telemetry for 45 days, while a separate store ingests the same data in parallel for longer retention. On the query side, performance is helped by metadata caching. When queries contain wildcards, previously resolved metadata is cached so subsequent queries matching the same pattern skip resolution and stay fast. Without that cache, every wildcard query would pay the full metadata-resolution cost and query latency would rise. To keep pace, the team continuously re-architects Argus rather than relying on a fixed design. OpenTSDB and HBase serve as core storage layers while metadata caching keeps wildcard query resolution fast on the serving path. Horizontal scaling and targeted tuning across each layer ensure the system handles the volume because solving one limit usually means preparing for the next. A look at the previous architecture. What reliability risks did Argus face operating in a single AWS region?how did that model risk complete unavailability during incidents? For years, the biggest reliability risk involved operating Argus in a single AWS region. While the team solved most internal software issues directly, a regional infrastructure outage created a dependency outside its control. If that AWS region failed, Argus visibility could suffer as a result. Beyond availability, the single-region model also drove up data transfer cost and latency, since telemetry from all other FIs/DCs/regions had to be shipped into this one central FI/region for processing. Argus powers dashboards and metrics across Salesforce, so teams rely on it during incidents to isolate failures and coordinate recovery. The risk was not a regional outage itself, rather, it was that one region could take down visibility globally, which is precisely the blast radius geo-local was designed to contain. A regional incident in that one region could render the entire platform unavailable — its blast radius extended across all of Argus at once, with no isolation between what failed and what remained available. Providing high availability by keeping multiple copies of Argus data across the regions was expensive at Argus scale because the system already consumed substantial AWS resources. Reducing that blast radius required a redesign that was both technically and economically viable. What architectural hurdles did the team face redesigning Argus into a multi-geo platform while controlling infrastructure cost? The transition to a multi-geo architecture required a major redesign rather than a simple deployment expansion. It was a six-month long effort that brought three teams together — Argus, Argus India, and the HBase team — spanning storage, and ingestion layers. The team required a model that improved resilience without making blast radius improvements too expensive. Instead of full replication, Argus introduced a geo-local model that distributes data across multiple production geographies. Metrics undergo processing and storage closer to their origin, which reduces cross-region dependencies and improves fault isolation. This shift required rethinking data placement, ingestion ownership, and regional responsibilities. The system also had to preserve existing functionality so internal dashboards and workflows continued without disruption. By distributing data intelligently rather than duplicating everything, the team created a practical path towards blast radius reduction while maintaining cost discipline. This is now live across 4 of 5 production regions, with only the final region remaining, completing our production rollout. A look at the latest architecture. What distributed systems complexities emerged when queries began spanning multiple geographies, especially around latency, partial results, and consistent user experience? When data spans multiple geographies, read paths become more complex than in a centralized model. A previous request succeeded or failed against one region. Now, some geographies may respond while another remains unavailable. This creates an operating model that requires the correct handling of partial data. The team introduced a federation query layer to address this challenge. This layer routes requests to regional query services, retrieves local results, and aggregates them for the caller. To route intelligently rather than broadcasting every query to every geography, the federation layer maintains metric scope to region-level metadata from all geographies, giving it a global view of where data actually lives. Backed by Elasticsearch mappings, this lets the federation layer resolve a query to only the relevant geographies and skip the rest. This avoids unnecessary cross-region fan-out, reduces load, and cuts latency on every request. Latency also presented a concern. Cross-region hops introduce delays for near-real-time workloads. The team optimized performance so users gained resiliency without facing unacceptable response times. The user experience evolved to match these technical shifts. Instead of silent failures, the system introduced partial-response semantics and HTTP 206 responses. UI signals now inform users when a geography becomes unavailable. This combination of federation, transparency, and graceful degradation makes multi-geo observability practical. What engineering demands remain to further shrink blast radius as telemetry volume continues to grow? With geo-local now live in production across nearly all regions, the focus shifts from rollout to sustaining isolation as volume grows. As demand rises, isolation boundaries require constant maintenance to keep any single failure from widening its reach. Each year brings more services, distributed workloads, and telemetry sources that increase the load on ingestion and storage. Recent AI adoption accelerates this trend. As AI workloads scale, existing instrumented code paths are exercised far more heavily, generating a much higher volume of signals. The observability platform must grow alongside the systems it monitors. Keeping blast radius small requires continuous capacity planning and architecture reviews. The team identifies future bottlenecks in storage and network paths before users feel an impact. This work requires disciplined operations. Multi-region systems reduce the blast radius of any single regional incident but introduce challenges around geo balancing and cross-region traffic costs. Sustaining fault isolation at this scale remains an ongoing engineering practice of constant adaptation. Learn more Stay connected — join our Talent Community ! Check out our Technology and Product teams to learn how you can get involved.

title: How to Improve Rootly Incident Response Automation with AI
summary: Close Rootly's investigation gap with Struct. Get AI-powered root-cause analysis in under 5 minutes and cut MTTR across your on-call stack. Try free.
body_text: Written by: Nimesh Chakravarthi, Co-founder & CTO, Struct Key Takeaways Rootly excels at coordination but leaves a 30-45 minute manual investigation gap that inflates MTTR across tools like Datadog and Sentry. Struct delivers AI-powered root-cause analysis in under five minutes by automatically correlating logs, traces, metrics, and code changes. Mapping Struct investigations to Rootly severity tiers ensures responders receive a complete report the moment they join an incident channel. Bi-directional Jira sync and automated status updates turn Rootly tickets into full post-incident artifacts without manual copy-paste. Struct layered on Rootly converts coordination into a complete end-to-end automated response loop for your on-call runbook. Designing Rootly Severity-Specific Workflows with Struct Rootly’s severity-based triggers determine which playbook fires, who gets paged, and what Slack channels open. However, most configurations lack a critical component: an automated investigation action that runs in parallel with these coordination steps. Without this parallel investigation, responders join the incident channel and must start their diagnostic work from scratch. Mapping a Struct investigation rule to each severity tier solves this gap by ensuring a root-cause report is already waiting when responders arrive. The table below shows how to pair each Rootly severity tier with the appropriate Struct investigation depth so responders receive actionable root-cause data as soon as they enter the incident channel. Configure Rootly triggers first, then attach the corresponding Struct rule to the same severity field. Alert Severity Rootly Trigger Struct Automated Investigation Action Expected Output Time SEV-1 (Critical) Immediate page + war-room channel creation Full stack investigation: logs, traces, code diff, blast-radius summary < 5 minutes SEV-2 (High) On-call page + incident Slack thread Targeted log correlation + anomaly timeline posted to thread < 5 minutes SEV-3 (Medium) Slack notification, no immediate page Lightweight triage: error rate delta + top exception summary < 5 minutes SEV-4 (Low) Ticket creation only Async investigation report attached to Jira ticket < 10 minutes Turning Rootly Jira Tickets into Full Incident Records Rootly’s native Jira integration creates tickets from incidents and can push status updates back to the incident record. The practical limitation is that the Jira ticket typically contains only coordination metadata, such as who is on call, what the severity is, and when it was acknowledged. It rarely contains investigation evidence. When Struct completes an automated investigation, it outputs a structured report that includes root cause, correlated log excerpts, impacted services, and a suggested fix. Routing that report into the linked Jira ticket, either via Rootly’s webhook or Struct’s direct Jira integration, turns the ticket into a complete post-incident artifact without any manual copy-paste. Engineers reviewing the ticket in a post-mortem have the full evidence chain. Product managers tracking SLA compliance have the blast-radius summary. The bi-directional sync then allows status changes in Jira, such as “Root Cause Identified”, to update the Rootly incident record, which keeps both systems consistent without duplicate effort. Feeding Investigation Results into Rootly Status Updates Rootly’s status-page and stakeholder-update automations work best when they carry investigation content, not just coordination status. A status update that reads “Investigating — engineers engaged” provides less value than one that reads “Investigating — elevated error rate on payment-service traced to a bad deploy at 14:32 UTC, rollback in progress.” Struct’s impact summary, generated within minutes of alert fire, can be injected into Rootly’s automated status update template via webhook. Stakeholder communications then reflect actual investigation findings rather than generic placeholders. This reduces inbound “what’s happening?” Slack messages to the on-call team and frees responders to focus on resolution rather than communication. Integrate AI Investigation with Rootly: Six-Step Playbook This six-step sequence assumes Rootly is already configured with at least one active severity workflow and that the engineering team uses Slack as the primary incident channel. Step 1 — Connect Rootly Slack Channel to Struct. Goal: give Struct a clear trigger source for new incidents. Owner: SRE lead. Input: Rootly incident Slack channel name. Output: Struct monitors the channel for new incident threads and starts investigations when they appear. Trade-off: Struct listens to all messages in the channel, so scope it to incident-creation bot messages only to reduce noise. Step 2 — Map Incident Fields. Goal: pass severity, service name, and alert body to Struct in a structured format. Owner: SRE lead. Input: Rootly incident payload schema. Output: Struct receives structured metadata alongside the raw alert, which improves correlation quality. Trade-off: custom field names in Rootly require a one-time mapping configuration in Struct. Step 3 — Configure Severity-Based Investigation Rules. Goal: match the severity-automation table above so that each Rootly severity tier triggers the appropriate Struct investigation depth. Owner: SRE lead or on-call engineer. Input: severity tiers defined in Rootly. Output: Struct runs the appropriate investigation depth per tier automatically. Trade-off: over-configuring SEV-3 and SEV-4 rules can generate investigation volume that exceeds the monthly plan limit on lower tiers, so start with SEV-1 and SEV-2 rules only and expand coverage once you have validated the investigation quality. Step 4 — Set Up Bi-Directional Jira Sync. Goal: route Struct’s investigation report into the linked Jira ticket and keep statuses aligned. Owner: engineering manager. Input: Jira project key and Rootly–Jira webhook. Output: every Struct report appends to the corresponding Jira issue, and Jira status changes reflect back in Rootly. Trade-off: this step requires Jira admin access to configure the inbound webhook. Step 5 — Enable Conversational Slack Bot. Goal: allow responders to query Struct mid-incident without leaving Slack. Owner: on-call engineer. Input: Struct bot added to the incident channel. Output: engineers tag Struct to pull additional logs, test hypotheses, or verify user impact interactively. Trade-off: junior engineers may over-rely on conversational queries instead of reviewing the initial report first. Step 6 — Route Resolved Root Causes to Code Agent or PR Creation. Goal: close the loop from alert to fix with minimal handoff friction. Owner: on-call engineer. Input: confirmed root cause from Struct dashboard. Output: Struct hands off context to a coding agent or generates a pull request directly. Trade-off: automated PR creation requires GitHub write access and a review gate to prevent unreviewed merges. Walk through this six-step setup in a live 10-minute demo to see how Struct automates your investigation workflow. Rootly MTTR Reduction Strategies with Struct MTTR is the sum of detection time, triage time, and resolution time. Rootly’s automation compresses detection time by paging faster and resolution time by coordinating responders. Triage time, the 30-to-45-minute window of manual investigation, remains largely untouched by coordination tooling alone. Large-scale Struct customers report an 80% reduction in triage time , for example, compressing a typical 45-minute investigation to under 5 minutes. Struct can help recover substantial engineer time monthly from triage alone, which returns hours to product development. A practical 30-day review cadence keeps these gains measurable. In week one, establish baseline MTTA and MTTR from Rootly’s incident analytics. In weeks two and three, run Struct on all SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents and log investigation completion time per event. In week four, compare triage duration before and after, and adjust severity rules where Struct’s investigation depth is mismatched to the alert type. U.S. teams operating under HIPAA or SOC 2 audit requirements should document this cadence as part of their incident response procedure (see FAQ for compliance details). Rootly Event-Driven Automations in Existing Stacks Achieving these MTTR reductions depends on how well the Rootly-plus-Struct workflow integrates with your existing observability stack. The combined workflow fits into existing observability stacks without requiring a platform migration. Struct integrates with Datadog, Sentry, AWS CloudWatch, GCP Logs, Azure Logs, Grafana, Prometheus, Loki, Sumo Logic, and Better Stack on the observability side, and with GitHub for code context. Rootly continues to own coordination, and Struct owns investigation, so neither system needs to replace the other. Three common pitfalls degrade the quality of event-driven automations in this setup, each representing a different form of insufficient signal: missing data, over-specified data, or unused institutional knowledge. First, incomplete telemetry: if services lack structured logging or trace IDs, Struct’s correlation engine has less signal to work with. The fix is to enforce trace ID propagation and structured log formats before enabling auto-investigations on those services. Second, over-customization: teams that write highly specific runbook instructions for every alert type spend more time maintaining Struct configurations than they save. This creates a different signal problem, with too much noise in the configuration layer. Start with general runbook ingestion and add specificity only where investigation accuracy is measurably low. Third, lack of runbook ingestion: Struct can ingest existing on-call runbooks directly, encoding institutional knowledge that would otherwise live only in senior engineers’ heads. This is the inverse of the over-customization problem, where teams have valuable signal but are not feeding it to the system. Teams that skip this step get generic investigations, while teams that complete it get investigations that mirror how their best SRE would approach the problem. Frequently Asked Questions Is Struct secure enough for teams with HIPAA or SOC 2 requirements? Struct is fully SOC 2 and HIPAA compliant. Logs are accessed and processed ephemerally, and they are not stored after the investigation completes. For the majority of Seed-to-Series C companies operating under these compliance frameworks, Struct meets the standard without additional configuration. How long does it take to set up Struct alongside Rootly? The initial setup of Rootly takes about 15 minutes . The integration playbook described above, including Jira sync and severity rule configuration, can be completed by one SRE. What happens if our logging and telemetry are incomplete? Struct’s investigation quality is proportional to the telemetry available. Teams already using Sentry, Datadog or cloud logs, and Slack for alerting get the highest investigation accuracy. If structured logging or trace IDs are absent for a given service, Struct will surface what it can but will note the data gap in the investigation report, which itself is a useful signal for improving observability coverage. Can we customize how Struct investigates our specific alert types? Yes. Teams can paste their existing on-call runbooks directly into Struct, define custom correlation ID formats, and configure composable widgets that guarantee specific data visualizations appear for certain alert categories. The AI follows the runbook logic when an alert fires and replicates the investigation approach of a senior engineer familiar with the system. Conclusion: Turning Rootly into a Full Response Loop Rootly is a strong coordination platform, but it does not eliminate the manual investigation window that consumes the majority of MTTR. Struct fills that gap by delivering zero-click root-cause context before responders engage , automatically correlating logs, traces, and code the moment an alert fires. The six-step integration playbook above converts Rootly from a coordination tool into a complete automated response loop. Alert fires, Rootly pages, Struct investigates, the responder reviews a five-minute report instead of hunting for 45 minutes, and the fix ships. Setup is fast, and you can see the FAQ for timing details. The platform is SOC 2 and HIPAA compliant. The 30-day pilot is risk-free.
